content: Niemann-Pick disease, type C1 (NPC1), is a disorder caused by mutations in a membrane protein responsible for intracellular cholesterol trafficking in mammals. In humans, this protein is encoded by the NPC1 gene, which is located on chromosome 18q11. Mutations in the NPC1 gene result in Niemann-Pick disease, type C, a rare autosomal recessive neurovisceral lipid storage disorder. This condition disrupts intracellular lipid transport, leading to the accumulation of lipid products in late endosomes and lysosomes. Approximately 95% of patients with Niemann-Pick disease, type C, have mutations in the NPC1 gene. The NPC1 protein is an integral membrane protein with sequence motifs that suggest its role in transporting cholesterol to post-lysosomal destinations. Obesity Mutations in the NPC1 gene have been strongly associated with obesity. A genome-wide association study identified NPC1 mutations as a significant risk factor for childhood obesity and adult morbid obesity. This study compared individuals with obesity to 1,416 age-matched individuals of normal weight. Additionally, NPC1 mutations have been linked to ordinary weight gain in the general population. Research in mice has shown that the NPC1 gene plays a role in appetite regulation. Mice with a non-functional NPC1 gene experience late-onset weight loss and reduced food intake. It is estimated that NPC1 gene variants may account for approximately 10% of childhood obesity cases and 14% of adult morbid obesity cases. HIV-AIDS Cholesterol pathways are critical at multiple stages of the HIV-1 infection cycle. Processes such as HIV-1 fusion, entry, assembly, and budding occur in cholesterol-enriched microdomains known as lipid rafts. The HIV-1 accessory protein Nef has been shown to upregulate genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis and homeostasis. Intracellular cholesterol trafficking pathways mediated by NPC1 are essential for efficient HIV-1 production. Ebola Virus The NPC1 cholesterol transporter is crucial for Ebola virus infection. Multiple independent studies have demonstrated that Ebola virus enters human cells by binding to NPC1. Laboratory experiments using cells from Niemann-Pick type C patients, who lack functional NPC1, showed that these cells were resistant to Ebola virus infection. This indicates that the virus relies on NPC1 to enter cells. Similar findings were observed with the Marburg virus, another filovirus, which also requires NPC1 for cell entry. One study revealed that NPC1 facilitates filovirus entry by directly binding to the viral envelope glycoprotein. A subsequent study confirmed that the second lysosomal domain of NPC1 mediates this binding. In one of the original studies, a small molecule was found to inhibit Ebola virus infection by preventing the viral glycoprotein from binding to NPC1. Another study demonstrated that mice heterozygous for NPC1 were protected from lethal Ebola virus infection. Collectively, these findings suggest that NPC1 could be a potential therapeutic target for developing antiviral drugs against Ebola. Mechanisms in Pathology In a mouse model with the mutation underlying Niemann-Pick type C1 disease, the expression of Myelin gene Regulatory Factor (MRF) was significantly reduced. MRF is a transcription factor essential for the development and maintenance of myelin sheaths. This reduction in MRF expression suggests that impaired oligodendrocyte maturation and disrupted myelination processes may contribute to the neurological deficits observed in Niemann-Pick type C1 disease.
